blocks.text: 1. Research Assistant
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061935-367329317.png

Code Assistant closed by pointing out that general programming questions with no specific codebase need no retrieval at all. Research Assistant, a RAG system design for synthesizing information across many, varied sources, tackles the opposite kind of question, one where retrieval does the most work.
It gathers and combines facts from several documents into one coherent, well cited synthesis.
2. The Design Problem's Scope
A research question rarely has its full answer in a single retrieved chunk.
The system must combine partial facts from several different sources into one coherent answer.

blocks.text: 3. Decomposing A Broad Question Into Sub-Questions

blocks.alt: Decomposing A Broad Question Into Sub-Questions
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061935-447856903.png
Similar to decomposing the goal into steps as covered in Planning, a broad research question breaks down into several narrower sub-questions, each independently answerable.
Each sub-question gets its own retrieval pass before the results are combined.
4. Multi-Query Retrieval Gathers Wider Evidence
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061935-852489944.png
As with generating multiple query variations in Fusion RAG, each sub-question becomes its own retrieval query, run independently against the source corpus.
The combined evidence covers far more ground than one single retrieval pass ever could.
5. Synthesizing Across Sources That Might Disagree

blocks.alt: Synthesizing Across Sources That Might Disagree
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061935-247650098.png
Much like the conflicting triples needing a resolution rule in Graph Construction, different sources can present conflicting facts on the same question.
The synthesis step must surface that disagreement rather than silently picking one side.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Two sources reporting different figures for the same statistic should both be mentioned in the synthesis with their sources noted, rather than the system silently choosing one and hiding the disagreement.

blocks.text: 6. Citing Every Source Used In The Synthesis

blocks.alt: Citing Every Source Used In The Synthesis
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448061935-225473149.png
Building on the citation format consistency covered in Citation Prompting, a synthesized answer combining five sources needs each individual claim traceable back to its own source.
A single blanket citation at the end is not precise enough for real research use.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Citation style","Precision for research use"],"rows":[["One blanket citation at the end","Not precise enough to trace individual claims"],["Per-claim citation","Each fact traceable to its specific source"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Iterative Refinement For Follow-Up Directions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448212518-663151341.png
As with the recursive decomposition of the query covered in Recursive RAG, a first synthesis often reveals a new, narrower question worth investigating further.
The system can recursively retrieve again on that newly surfaced sub-topic.
8. Longer Synthesis Tasks Can Be Worth Higher Latency
As Latency Optimization establishes, latency targets depend on the use case, and a deep research task tolerates a much longer response time than a quick factual lookup.
Thorough multi-source synthesis is worth the wait for this specific use case.
9. Recognizing When This Research Assistant Design Fits The Actual Need

blocks.alt: Recognizing When This Research Assistant Design Fits The Actual Need
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448212520-468123041.png
A broad question needing synthesis across many sources fits this design.
A single, precise factual lookup fits a simpler naive RAG pipeline better instead.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Treating a broad research question as answerable with a single retrieval pass.
Silently picking one source when two sources disagree on the same fact.
Attaching one blanket citation to a multi-source synthesis instead of citing each claim.
Rushing latency optimization on a deep research task that users actually expect to take longer.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: A research assistant synthesizes information across many, varied sources into one coherent answer.
A broad research question rarely has its full answer in a single retrieved chunk.
Decomposing the question into sub-questions lets each get its own independent retrieval pass.
Multi-query retrieval across sub-questions covers far more ground than one single pass.
Sources that disagree should have that disagreement surfaced, not silently resolved one way.
A multi-source synthesis needs per-claim citation, not one blanket citation at the end.
A first synthesis can reveal a narrower follow-up question worth recursively investigating.
Deep research tasks tolerate much higher latency than a quick factual lookup would.
